## Today's Data: Student Survey {style="font-size:65%"}

168 intro statistics students at the University of Adelaide filled out a survey and had a few things measured. This is a cleaned version of `MASS::survey` that keeps only students with complete records. [Download survey_data.csv](data/survey_data.csv)

| Variable | Description |
|----|----|
| `id` | Student identifier |
| `sex` | Student sex (female, male) |
| `hand` | Writing hand (left, right) |
| `smoke` | How much the student smokes (never, occasional, regular, heavy) |
| `exercise` | How often the student exercises (none, some, freq = frequently) |
| `age` | Age (years) |
| `height` | Height (cm) |
| `pulse` | Pulse rate (beats per minute) |
| `wr_hand` | Span of the **writing** hand, tip of thumb to tip of little finger (cm) |
| `nw_hand` | Span of the **non-writing** hand (cm) |

::: notes
survey_data.csv was made from MASS::survey: keep Sex, W.Hnd, Exer, Smoke, Age, Height, Pulse, Wr.Hnd, NW.Hnd; drop rows with any NA (237 -\> 168); rename to lowercase; age rounded to 1 decimal.
:::

# Part 1: Correlation & Regression {.center}

## Research Question 1 {style="font-size:85%"}

Bigger people tend to have bigger hands.

**How strongly is a student's writing-hand span related to their height, and can hand span be used to predict height?**

::: fragment
| Role                             | Variable  |
|:---------------------------------|:----------|
| Outcome (*y*, vertical axis)     | `height`  |
| Predictor (*x*, horizontal axis) | `wr_hand` |
:::

::: fragment
Two continuous variables → **correlation** (how strongly related?) and **simple linear regression** (can *x* predict *y*?)
:::

## 1.1 Import & Get a Sense of the Data {style="font-size:80%"}

```{r}
library(tidyverse)   # ggplot2 for plots, dplyr for group summaries
library(car)         # leveneTest() for Part 3

survey <- read.csv("data/survey_data.csv")
```

::: panel-tabset
### `head()`

```{r}
head(survey)
```

### `str()`

```{r}
str(survey)
```

### `summary()`

```{r}
summary(survey[, c("age", "height", "pulse", "wr_hand", "nw_hand")])
```
:::

::: {style="font-size:80%"}
ⓘ The file path is relative to your `.Rmd`, so keep the CSV in the same folder (or a `data/` subfolder). Other options: `dim()`, `names()`, `glimpse()`, `psych::describe()`
:::

## 1.1 Put the Groups in a Sensible Order {style="font-size:85%"}

R reads text columns as characters and sorts groups **alphabetically**:

```{r}
table(survey$exercise)
```

::: fragment
`factor()` with `levels =` sets the order *you* want (none → some → freq):

```{r}
survey$exercise <- factor(survey$exercise, levels = c("none", "some", "freq"))
table(survey$exercise)
```
:::

::::: fragment
::: subpoint
○ Run it **once, right after importing**, so every table, plot, ANOVA, and Tukey output in Part 3 reads in a natural order
:::

::: subpoint
○ Spelling must match the data exactly: a misspelled level turns those rows into `NA`
:::
:::::

## Correlation: The Big Idea {style="font-size:85%"}

**Pearson's** $r$: the direction and strength of the **linear** relationship between two continuous variables, from −1 to +1

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(13)
make_r <- function(r, n = 120) {
  x <- rnorm(n)
  data.frame(x = x, y = r * x + sqrt(1 - r^2) * rnorm(n))
}
x_curve <- runif(120, -2, 2)
sims <- bind_rows(
  make_r(-0.8) |> mutate(panel = 1),
  make_r(0)    |> mutate(panel = 2),
  make_r(0.4)  |> mutate(panel = 3),
  make_r(0.9)  |> mutate(panel = 4),
  data.frame(x = x_curve, y = x_curve^2 + rnorm(120, 0, .3), panel = 5)
)
panel_labels <- sims |>
  group_by(panel) |>
  summarise(r = cor(x, y)) |>
  mutate(label = sprintf("r = %.2f", r),
         label = ifelse(panel == 5, paste0(label, " (curved!)"), label))
sims |>
  left_join(panel_labels, by = "panel") |>
  mutate(label = fct_reorder(label, panel)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(color = "#5a55fa", alpha = .6, size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ label, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"))
```

::: subpoint
○ **Sign** = direction: + both rise together; − one rises as the other falls
:::

::: subpoint
○ **Size** (how close to ±1) = strength: how tightly points hug a straight line
:::

::: subpoint
○ $r$ only sees straight lines: the last panel has a strong pattern but $r \approx 0$, so **always plot first**
:::

:::

What do you see? Points rise from left to right, in a fairly tight cloud with no curve
:::

## 1.3 Correlation Coefficient {style="font-size:80%"}

```{r}
cor(survey$wr_hand, survey$height)
```

::: subpoint
○ Order doesn't matter: `cor(x, y)` = `cor(y, x)`
:::

::: fragment
Under the hood, $r$ is the **average product of z-scores**:

$$r = \frac{\sum z_x z_y}{n - 1}$$

```{r}
z_hand   <- (survey$wr_hand - mean(survey$wr_hand)) / sd(survey$wr_hand)
z_height <- (survey$height  - mean(survey$height))  / sd(survey$height)
sum(z_hand * z_height) / (nrow(survey) - 1)
```
:::

## Why Does *r* Come Out Positive? {style="font-size:85%"}

::::::::: columns
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 5.4
quad <- survey |>
  mutate(zx = (wr_hand - mean(wr_hand)) / sd(wr_hand),
         zy = (height - mean(height)) / sd(height),
         product = ifelse(zx * zy > 0, "positive", "negative"))
ggplot(quad, aes(x = wr_hand, y = height, color = product)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(survey$wr_hand), linetype = "dashed", color = "gray60") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(survey$height), linetype = "dashed", color = "gray60") +
  geom_point(size = 2.8, alpha = .7) +
  annotate("text", x = 23.4, y = 203, label = "(+)(+) = +", color = "#5a55fa", size = 6, fontface = "bold", hjust = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 12.8, y = 149, label = "(-)(-) = +", color = "#5a55fa", size = 6, fontface = "bold", hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 12.8, y = 203, label = "(-)(+) = -", color = "#b04c19", size = 6, fontface = "bold", hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 23.4, y = 149, label = "(+)(-) = -", color = "#b04c19", size = 6, fontface = "bold", hjust = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(positive = "#5a55fa", negative = "#b04c19")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(12.8, 23.4), ylim = c(148, 204)) +
  labs(x = "Writing-hand span (cm)", y = "Height (cm)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
:::

::::::: {.column width="38%"}
Dashed lines = the two means

::: subpoint
○ Above-average hand **and** above-average height: $(+)(+) = +$
:::

::: subpoint
○ Below on both: $(-)(-) = +$
:::

::: subpoint
○ Above on one, below on the other: product is $-$
:::

::: fragment
`r sum(quad$zx * quad$zy > 0)` of the 168 students land in a **+** quadrant, so the products add up to a positive $r$
:::
:::::::
:::::::::

## 1.4 Describing Direction & Strength {style="font-size:85%"}

::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="50%"}
**Direction** = sign of $r$

::: subpoint
○ $+$: as one goes up, so does the other
:::

::: subpoint
○ $-$: as one goes up, the other goes down
:::

**Strength** = size of $|r|$ (Cohen's rough guidelines)

| $|r|$ | Strength |
|:-----:|:--------:|
| ≈ .10 |   weak   |
| ≈ .30 | moderate |
| ≥ .50 |  strong  |
:::::

::::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
**Our result:** $r$ = .65 → **positive** and **strong**

::: my-callout
The scatterplot and $r$ = .65 show a strong, positive linear relationship between writing-hand span and height: students with wider hand spans tend to be taller.
:::

<br>

::: {style="font-size:80%"}
ⓘ Use **both** pieces of evidence: the plot shows the shape and any outliers, $r$ puts a number on it

ⓘ Correlation ≠ causation: stretching your hand won't make you taller!
:::
:::::
:::::::::

## 1.5 Correlation Matrix {style="font-size:80%"}

Give `cor()` several columns at once and it returns every pairwise correlation:

```{r}
round(cor(survey[, c("wr_hand", "nw_hand", "height", "pulse")]), 2)

# same thing with dplyr:
# survey |> select(wr_hand, nw_hand, height, pulse) |> cor() |> round(2)
```

::::::: columns
::::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
**How to read it**

::: subpoint
○ Diagonal = 1 (each variable with itself): skip it
:::

::: subpoint
○ The two triangles are mirror images: read just one
:::
:::::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
**Strongest** = largest $|r|$: `wr_hand` & `nw_hand` (.97), since your two hands are nearly the same size

**Weakest** = closest to 0: `wr_hand` & `pulse` (−.01), basically no relationship
:::
:::::::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:80%"}
ⓘ Strength ignores the sign: $r$ = −.08 is *stronger* than $r$ = −.01. If your data had missing values, add `use = "complete.obs"`
:::

## Regression: Drawing the Best Line {style="font-size:85%"}

::::::::: columns
::::::: {.column width="45%"}
$$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x$$

::: subpoint
○ $\hat{y}$ = predicted height
:::

::: subpoint
○ $b_0$ = **intercept**: predicted $y$ when $x = 0$
:::

::: subpoint
○ $b_1$ = **slope**: change in predicted $y$ for every 1-unit increase in $x$
:::

::: fragment
"Best" line = **least squares**: the line that makes the sum of squared residuals as small as possible

$$\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$$
:::
:::::::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5
fit_demo <- lm(height ~ wr_hand, data = survey)
survey |>
  mutate(pred = fitted(fit_demo)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = wr_hand, y = height)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = wr_hand, yend = pred), color = "#b04c19", alpha = .45) +
  geom_point(alpha = .6, size = 2.5) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(fit_demo)[1], slope = coef(fit_demo)[2],
              color = "#5a55fa", linewidth = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 22.4, y = 156, label = "red lines =\nresiduals", color = "#b04c19", size = 6) +
  labs(x = "Writing-hand span (cm)", y = "Height (cm)")
```
:::
:::::::::

## 1.6 Hypotheses for the Slope {style="font-size:85%"}

$H_0$: $\beta_1 = 0$

::: subpoint
○ Hand span does **not** predict height (the population line is flat)
:::

$H_1$: $\beta_1 \neq 0$

::: subpoint
○ Hand span **does** predict height (the population line has a nonzero slope)
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%"}
ⓘ $\beta_1$ (Greek) is the **population** slope we're testing; $b_1$ is the slope we **estimate** from our sample

ⓘ `lm()` tests this two-tailed by default
:::

## 1.7 Simple Linear Regression {style="font-size:80%"}

`lm(outcome ~ predictor, data = ...)`: same `y ~ x` formula as the plot

```{r}
height_model <- lm(height ~ wr_hand, data = survey)
summary(height_model)
```

## Reading the `summary()` Output {style="font-size:75%"}

::::::::::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
round(summary(height_model)$coefficients, 4)
summary(height_model)$r.squared
```
:::

::::::::::: {.column width="52%"}
::: subpoint
○ **Estimate**: $b_0$ = 108.95 (intercept), $b_1$ = 3.38 (slope)
:::

::: subpoint
○ **Std. Error**: how much each estimate would bounce around from sample to sample
:::

::: subpoint
○ **t value** = Estimate ÷ Std. Error (3.3785 ÷ 0.3057 = 11.05)
:::

::: subpoint
○ **Pr(\>\|t\|)**: *p*-value for $H_0: \beta = 0$
:::

::: subpoint
○ **df** = $n - 2$ = 166 (we estimated two things: $b_0$ and $b_1$)
:::

::::: fragment
::: subpoint
○ $R^2$ = .42: hand span explains 42% of the variability in height. With one predictor, $R^2 = r^2$ (.651² = .42)
:::

::: subpoint
○ The *F*-test at the bottom tests the whole model. With one predictor, $F = t^2$ (11.05² = 122.1)
:::
:::::
:::::::::::
:::::::::::::

## 1.8 Interpreting the Slope {style="font-size:85%"}

:::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="52%"}
Template: *For every 1-\[unit\] increase in \[x\], \[y\] is predicted to \[increase / decrease\] by \[*$b_1$\] \[units\].

::: {.my-callout .fragment}
For every **1-cm** increase in writing-hand span, predicted height increases by **3.38 cm**. The slope is significant, $b$ = 3.38, $t$(166) = 11.05, $p$ \< .001, so we reject $H_0$: hand span significantly predicts height.
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:80%"}
ⓘ The intercept (108.95 cm) is the predicted height for a hand span of **0 cm**. Nobody has a 0-cm hand, so the intercept just anchors the line. Don't over-interpret it
:::
:::::

:::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.8
ggplot(survey, aes(x = wr_hand, y = height)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#5a55fa", fill = "#5a55fa", alpha = .2, linewidth = 1.8) +
  labs(x = "Writing-hand span (cm)", y = "Height (cm)")
```

::: {style="font-size:70%"}
add `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` to draw the line
:::
::::
::::::::

## 1.9 Predicted Values {style="font-size:80%"}

What height would we predict for hand spans of **16, 18, and 20 cm**?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**By hand** with the coefficients: $\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x$

```{r}
b <- coef(height_model)
b
b[1] + b[2] * c(16, 18, 20)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**With `predict()`**

```{r}
new_hands <- data.frame(wr_hand = c(16, 18, 20))
predict(height_model, newdata = new_hands)
```
:::
:::::

:::::: fragment
::: subpoint
○ The column in `newdata` must have **exactly** the same name as the predictor (`wr_hand`)
:::

::: subpoint
○ Each extra 2 cm of hand span adds 2 × 3.38 = 6.76 cm of predicted height
:::

::: subpoint
○ Only predict inside the range you observed (13 to 23.2 cm here)
:::
::::::

## 1.10 z-Scores {style="font-size:80%"}

$$z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}$$

```{r}
survey$height_z  <- (survey$height - mean(survey$height)) / sd(survey$height)
survey$wr_hand_z <- as.numeric(scale(survey$wr_hand))   # scale() does the same thing

round(c(mean = mean(survey$height_z),  sd = sd(survey$height_z)), 2)
round(c(mean = mean(survey$wr_hand_z), sd = sd(survey$wr_hand_z)), 2)
```

::: subpoint
○ `scale()` returns a matrix, so wrap it in `as.numeric()` to store a plain column
:::

::: fragment
**Bonus:** regress one z-score on the other, and the slope **is** $r$

```{r}
round(coef(lm(height_z ~ wr_hand_z, data = survey)), 3)
```
:::

# Part 2: Paired *t*-Test {.center}

## Research Question 2 {style="font-size:85%"}

::::::::: columns
::::::: {.column width="50%"}
Most of us use our writing hand far more than the other one.

**Is a student's writing-hand span different from their non-writing-hand span?**

:::::: fragment
Every student has **two** scores, `wr_hand` and `nw_hand`, so the scores come in **pairs**

::: subpoint
○ above the dashed line: writing hand wider (`r sum(survey$wr_hand > survey$nw_hand)` students)
:::

::: subpoint
○ below: non-writing hand wider (`r sum(survey$wr_hand < survey$nw_hand)`)
:::

::: subpoint
○ on it: same span (`r sum(survey$wr_hand == survey$nw_hand)`)
:::
::::::
:::::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 5.5
ggplot(survey, aes(x = nw_hand, y = wr_hand)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_jitter(width = .08, height = .08, alpha = .5, size = 2.5, color = "#5a55fa") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Non-writing-hand span (cm)", y = "Writing-hand span (cm)")
```
:::
:::::::::

## 2.1 Hypotheses {style="font-size:85%"}

For each student, $D$ = `wr_hand` − `nw_hand`

$H_0$: $\mu_D = 0$

::: subpoint
○ On average, the two hands have the same span
:::

$H_1$: $\mu_D \neq 0$

::: subpoint
○ On average, the two hands' spans differ
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%"}
ⓘ Hypotheses are about the **population** mean difference ($\mu_D$), not our sample's $\bar{d}$
:::

## 2.2 Which Test, and Why? {style="font-size:85%"}

**Paired-samples (dependent) *t*-test, two-tailed**

::: subpoint
○ **Paired**: the same 168 students give both measurements, so each `wr_hand` score is matched to one `nw_hand` score. These are not two independent groups
:::

::: subpoint
○ **Two-tailed**: the question asks whether the spans are **different**, not whether one is **larger**
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%"}
| Same people (or matched units) measured twice? | Number of groups / conditions | Test |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Yes | 2 | Paired-samples *t* |
| No | 2 | Independent-samples *t* |
| No | 3 or more | One-way ANOVA |

Direction stated in the question ("higher," "decrease") → one-tailed. Just "different" → two-tailed
:::

## 2.3 Means and the Difference Between Them {style="font-size:85%"}

```{r}
mean_wr <- mean(survey$wr_hand)
mean_nw <- mean(survey$nw_hand)

mean_wr
mean_nw
mean_wr - mean_nw
```

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%"}
ⓘ When a question says **display** the result, save it **and** print it. Shortcut: wrapping an assignment in parentheses does both, e.g., `(mean_wr <- mean(survey$wr_hand))`
:::

## 2.4 A Difference Score for Each Student {style="font-size:80%"}

::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
survey$hand_diff <- survey$wr_hand - survey$nw_hand
head(survey[, c("id", "wr_hand", "nw_hand", "hand_diff")])
```

::: subpoint
○ Keep the same order as 2.3 (writing − non-writing), so a **positive** difference = writing hand wider
:::

::: subpoint
○ Two columns are now **one**, so a paired *t*-test is a one-sample *t*-test of `hand_diff` against 0
:::
:::::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4.6
ggplot(survey, aes(x = hand_diff)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = .2, fill = "#5a55fa", alpha = .7, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Writing minus non-writing span (cm)", y = "Number of students")
```
:::
:::::::

## 2.5–2.7 Mean, SD, and SE of the Differences {style="font-size:80%"}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r}
n         <- nrow(survey)             # number of pairs
mean_diff <- mean(survey$hand_diff)   # 2.5
sd_diff   <- sd(survey$hand_diff)     # 2.6
se_diff   <- sd_diff / sqrt(n)        # 2.7

mean_diff
sd_diff
se_diff
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
$$\bar{d} = \frac{\sum d_i}{n}$$

$$s_d = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (d_i - \bar{d})^2}{n - 1}}$$

$$SE_{\bar{d}} = \frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}}$$
:::
:::::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%"}
ⓘ The mean of the differences = the difference of the means (0.0708 both ways, compare with 2.3)

ⓘ $n$ = number of **pairs** (168 students), not number of scores (336)
:::

## 2.8 Degrees of Freedom & Critical *t* {style="font-size:85%"}

$$df = n - 1 = 168 - 1 = 167$$

```{r}
df_t <- n - 1
qt(1 - .05/2, df = df_t)   # two-tailed: .025 in each tail
```

::: fragment
Reject $H_0$ if $|t| > 1.97$
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%"}
ⓘ Reminder from Lab 11: a one-tailed test puts all of $\alpha$ in one tail, `qt(.95, df = 167)` = 1.65
:::

## 2.9 Statistical Decision & Conclusion {style="font-size:80%"}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
$$t = \frac{\bar{d}}{SE_{\bar{d}}}$$

```{r}
t_obs <- mean_diff / se_diff
t_obs

2 * pt(-abs(t_obs), df = df_t)   # two-tailed p
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.8
#| fig-height: 3.8
crit_t <- qt(.975, df_t)
t_curve <- tibble(t = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 600), dens = dt(t, df_t))
ggplot(t_curve, aes(t, dens)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(t_curve, t >= crit_t), fill = "#b04c19", alpha = .5) +
  geom_area(data = filter(t_curve, t <= -crit_t), fill = "#b04c19", alpha = .5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = t_obs, color = "#5a55fa", linewidth = 1.6) +
  annotate("text", x = t_obs, y = .43, label = sprintf("t = %.2f", t_obs),
           color = "#5a55fa", size = 6, hjust = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = c(-3.1, 3.1), y = .08, label = c("-1.97", "+1.97"),
           color = "#b04c19", size = 5.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, .45), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "t (df = 167)", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
        axis.line.y = element_blank())
```
:::
:::::

::: fragment
**Decision:** $|1.77| < 1.97$ ($p$ = .078 \> .05) → **fail to reject** $H_0$
:::

::: {.my-callout .fragment}
**Conclusion:** Students' writing-hand span (*M* = 18.80 cm) was not significantly different from their non-writing-hand span (*M* = 18.73 cm), $t$(167) = 1.77, $p$ = .078.
:::

## 2.9 Double-Check with `t.test()` {style="font-size:80%"}

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
t.test(survey$wr_hand, survey$nw_hand, paired = TRUE)
```
:::

::::: {.column width="40%"}
Same $t$(167) = 1.77, $p$ = .078 ✓

::: fragment
95% CI for $\mu_D$: \[−0.01, 0.15\] **includes 0**, which agrees with failing to reject $H_0$
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%"}
ⓘ Order matters: R computes **first − second**, the same order as `hand_diff`

ⓘ Same result: `t.test(survey$hand_diff, mu = 0)`

ⓘ "Fail to reject" ≠ "the hands are identical." We just don't have enough evidence of a difference
:::
:::::
:::::::

## 2.10 Effect Size: Cohen's *d* {style="font-size:85%"}

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
$$d = \frac{\bar{d}}{s_d}$$

```{r}
cohens_d <- mean_diff / sd_diff
cohens_d
```

| $|d|$ |  Size  |
|:-----:|:------:|
|  0.2  | small  |
|  0.5  | medium |
|  0.8  | large  |
:::

::::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
::: my-callout
$d$ = 0.14 is below even the "small" benchmark of 0.2: the average difference between the two hands is only about one-seventh of a standard deviation. A **negligible** effect.
:::

<br>

::: {style="font-size:80%"}
ⓘ $t$ grows with $n$, but $d$ doesn't. $d$ tells you how **big** a difference is, no matter how many people you measured
:::
:::::
:::::::

# Part 3: One-Way ANOVA {.center}

## Research Question 3 {style="font-size:85%"}

People who exercise often tend to have lower heart rates.

**Does pulse rate differ across students who exercise not at all, some of the time, or frequently?**

::::: fragment
::: subpoint
○ Outcome: `pulse` (continuous)
:::

::: subpoint
○ Grouping variable: `exercise` (3 groups, already put in order back in 1.1)
:::

3 or more independent groups, one continuous outcome → **one-way ANOVA**
:::::

## 3.1 Hypotheses {style="font-size:85%"}

$H_0$: $\mu_{none} = \mu_{some} = \mu_{freq}$

::: subpoint
○ Average pulse is the same in all three exercise groups
:::

$H_1$: at least one group mean differs from the others

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%"}
⚠ Not $H_1: \mu_{none} \neq \mu_{some} \neq \mu_{freq}$. $H_1$ is true even if only **one** group stands out
:::

## 3.2 Descriptives by Group {style="font-size:80%"}

::::::::: columns
::::::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
survey |>
  group_by(exercise) |>
  summarise(n    = n(),
            mean = mean(pulse),
            sd   = sd(pulse))
```

::: {style="font-size:85%"}
Base R alternative:

`tapply(survey$pulse, survey$exercise, mean)`
:::

::::: fragment
::: subpoint
○ Frequent exercisers have the lowest average pulse
:::

::: subpoint
○ Group sizes are unequal (14 / 69 / 85). That's fine for ANOVA
:::
:::::
:::::::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(survey, aes(x = exercise, y = pulse, fill = exercise)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .5, outlier.shape = NA, width = .55) +
  geom_jitter(width = .12, height = 0, alpha = .4, size = 1.8) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 5, fill = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#b04c19", "#dfc127", "#5a55fa")) +
  labs(x = "Exercise", y = "Pulse (beats per minute)", caption = "white diamond = group mean") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
:::
:::::::::

## 3.3 Homogeneity of Variance {style="font-size:80%"}

ANOVA assumes the groups have (roughly) **equal variances**. Pick **one** method, name it, and state your conclusion

::: panel-tabset
### Rule of thumb

```{r}
group_sds <- tapply(survey$pulse, survey$exercise, sd)
group_sds
max(group_sds) / min(group_sds)
```

Largest SD ÷ smallest SD = 1.43, which is **less than 2** → assumption satisfied

### Levene's test

```{r}
leveneTest(pulse ~ exercise, data = survey)   # from the car package
```

$F$(2, 165) = 1.33, $p$ = .268 → **not significant** → assumption satisfied

ⓘ Install once in the console: `install.packages("car")`

### Bartlett's test

```{r}
bartlett.test(pulse ~ exercise, data = survey)   # base R
```

$p$ = .177 → **not significant** → assumption satisfied (Bartlett's is more sensitive to non-normal data than Levene's)
:::

::: {.my-callout .fragment}
Here a **non-significant** result is the good news: $H_0$ for these tests is that the variances are equal.
:::

## 3.4 Run the One-Way ANOVA {style="font-size:85%"}

`aov(outcome ~ group, data = ...)`, then `summary()`

```{r}
pulse_model <- aov(pulse ~ exercise, data = survey)
summary(pulse_model)
```

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%"}
ⓘ Check the `Df` next to your grouping variable: it should be (number of groups − 1) = 2. If it says **1**, R treated your groups as a number (e.g., groups coded 1/2/3). Convert with `factor()` first!
:::

## 3.5 Degrees of Freedom {style="font-size:85%"}

$k$ = 3 groups, $N$ = 168 students

|                | Formula |       Value       |
|:---------------|:-------:|:-----------------:|
| $df_{between}$ | $k - 1$ |   3 − 1 = **2**   |
| $df_{within}$  | $N - k$ | 168 − 3 = **165** |
| $df_{total}$   | $N - 1$ | 168 − 1 = **167** |

::: fragment
```{r}
k <- nlevels(survey$exercise)
N <- nrow(survey)
c(df_between = k - 1, df_within = N - k, df_total = N - 1)
```
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%"}
ⓘ $df_{between} + df_{within} = df_{total}$: 2 + 165 = 167
:::

## 3.6 Verify the Mean Squares {style="font-size:80%"}

$$MS = \frac{SS}{df} \qquad MS_{between} = \frac{SS_{between}}{k - 1} \qquad MS_{within} = \frac{SS_{within}}{N - k}$$

```{r}
anova_table <- summary(pulse_model)[[1]]   # the ANOVA table as a data frame
ss_between  <- anova_table$`Sum Sq`[1]
ss_within   <- anova_table$`Sum Sq`[2]

ms_between <- ss_between / (k - 1)
ms_within  <- ss_within  / (N - k)
c(ms_between = ms_between, ms_within = ms_within)
```

::: fragment
1153.27 ÷ 2 = **576.6** and 21076.64 ÷ 165 = **127.7** ✓ match the `Mean Sq` column
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%"}
ⓘ The printed table rounds SS (1153, 21077). Pulling the values out of the table object, as above, avoids rounding error
:::

## 3.7 Verify *F* {style="font-size:85%"}

$$F = \frac{MS_{between}}{MS_{within}}$$

```{r}
F_obs <- ms_between / ms_within
F_obs
```

::: fragment
576.6 ÷ 127.7 = **4.51** ✓ matches the `F value` column
:::

:::: fragment
::: subpoint
○ The variability **between** exercise groups is about 4.5 times the variability **within** them
:::
::::

## 3.8 Critical *F*, Decision & Conclusion {style="font-size:80%"}

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
# critical F
qf(.95, df1 = k - 1, df2 = N - k)

# p-value
pf(F_obs, k - 1, N - k, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

::: {style="font-size:85%"}
ⓘ *F* only has an upper tail (it's a ratio of variances), so use `.95`, not `.975`
:::
::::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 3.6
crit_F <- qf(.95, k - 1, N - k)
F_curve <- tibble(f = seq(0, 7, length.out = 600), dens = df(f, k - 1, N - k))
ggplot(F_curve, aes(f, dens)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(F_curve, f >= crit_F), fill = "#b04c19", alpha = .5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = F_obs, color = "#5a55fa", linewidth = 1.6) +
  annotate("text", x = F_obs, y = .8, label = sprintf("F = %.2f", F_obs),
           color = "#5a55fa", size = 6, hjust = -0.1) +
  annotate("text", x = crit_F, y = .25, label = sprintf("critical\nF = %.2f", crit_F),
           color = "#b04c19", size = 5, hjust = 1.1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.02), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "F (2, 165)", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
        axis.line.y = element_blank())
```
:::
::::::

::: fragment
**Decision:** 4.51 \> 3.05 ($p$ = .012 \< .05) → **reject** $H_0$
:::

::: {.my-callout .fragment}
**Conclusion:** Pulse rate differs significantly across exercise groups, $F$(2, 165) = 4.51, $p$ = .012. ANOVA tells us **some** difference exists, but not **which** groups differ → Tukey's HSD
:::

## 3.9 Tukey's HSD: All Pairwise Comparisons {style="font-size:75%"}

```{r}
TukeyHSD(pulse_model)
```

:::::::: columns
:::::: {.column .fragment width="40%"}
::: subpoint
○ `diff` = first group's mean − second group's mean
:::

::: subpoint
○ `lwr`, `upr` = 95% CI, adjusted for making 3 comparisons
:::

::: subpoint
○ `p adj` \< .05 (CI excludes 0) → significant
:::
::::::

::: {.column .fragment width="60%"}
| Comparison  | Diff. (bpm) | $p$ adj | Significant? |
|:------------|:-----------:|:-------:|:------------:|
| some − none |    0.97     |  .954   |      no      |
| freq − none |    −4.41    |  .368   |      no      |
| freq − some |    −5.38    |  .011   |   **yes**    |
:::
::::::::

## 3.9 What's the Pattern? {style="font-size:80%"}

::::::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.6
par(mar = c(4.5, 7, 2.5, 1))
plot(TukeyHSD(pulse_model), las = 1)
```
:::

::::::: {.column width="50%"}
::: subpoint
○ Frequent exercisers have the lowest pulse (*M* = 71.45), significantly lower than the "some" group (*M* = 76.83)
:::

::: subpoint
○ The "none" group (*M* = 75.86) did not differ significantly from either group. With only 14 students, its confidence intervals are very wide
:::

::: fragment
**Overall:** exercising *frequently*, not just *sometimes*, goes with a lower pulse
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%"}
ⓘ Not significant ≠ no difference: small groups have low power

ⓘ This is survey data, not an experiment, so we can't say exercise **causes** a lower pulse
:::
:::::::
:::::::::

## 3.10 Writing It Up in APA Style {style="font-size:75%"}

Include: the test, $F$($df_{between}$, $df_{within}$), $p$, each group's *M* and *SD*, and what Tukey's HSD showed, in full sentences

::: {.my-callout .fragment}
A one-way ANOVA was conducted to examine whether pulse rate differed by how often students exercised. Pulse rate differed significantly across exercise groups, *F*(2, 165) = 4.51, *p* = .012. Students who exercised frequently (*M* = 71.45, *SD* = 11.00) had a lower average pulse than students who exercised some of the time (*M* = 76.83, *SD* = 10.74) or not at all (*M* = 75.86, *SD* = 15.38). Tukey's HSD post hoc comparisons showed that the frequent group's pulse was significantly lower than the some group's (*p* = .011). The no-exercise group did not differ significantly from either the some group (*p* = .954) or the frequent group (*p* = .368).
:::

::::::: fragment
**APA 7 reminders**

::: subpoint
○ Italicize statistical symbols: *F*, *t*, *r*, *p*, *M*, *SD*
:::

::: subpoint
○ No leading zero for values that can't exceed 1: *p* = .012, *r* = .65 (but *M* = 0.07)
:::

::: subpoint
○ Report exact *p* to 2–3 decimals; write *p* \< .001 when it's tiny
:::

::: subpoint
○ Optional extra: effect size $\eta^2 = SS_{between} / SS_{total}$ = 1153.27 / 22229.90 = .05
:::
:::::::

## Exam Survival Checklist {style="font-size:78%"}

::::::::::::::::: columns
:::::::: {.column width="50%"}
**R & RMarkdown**

::: subpoint
○ Knit early and often: one error anywhere stops the knit
:::

::: subpoint
○ Every object must be created **inside** the `.Rmd` (code you ran only in the console doesn't count)
:::

::: subpoint
○ Keep the CSV next to your `.Rmd` and import it with `read.csv("file.csv")`
:::

::: subpoint
○ Run `install.packages()` in the console, never in the `.Rmd`
:::

::: subpoint
○ Print every value you're asked to calculate or display
:::
::::::::

:::::::::: {.column width="50%"}
**Statistics**

::: subpoint
○ Run `factor()` right after importing
:::

::: subpoint
○ Scatterplot: outcome on the *y*-axis (`y ~ x`)
:::

::: subpoint
○ Strength of *r* = size of $|r|$; skip the diagonal of the matrix
:::

::: subpoint
○ Paired *t*: $n$ = number of pairs; keep the difference order consistent
:::

::: subpoint
○ Say "fail to reject $H_0$," never "accept $H_0$"
:::

::: subpoint
○ ANOVA $H_1$: "at least one mean differs"
:::

::: subpoint
○ Always follow a decision with a plain-English conclusion
:::
::::::::::

## Extra Practice: Penguins {style="font-size:78%"}

Same steps, new data: `palmerpenguins` (you met them in Lab 12)

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(palmerpenguins)
penguins <- na.omit(penguins)   # drop rows with missing values (333 penguins left)
```

1.  **Part 1 steps:** How strongly is `flipper_length_mm` related to `bill_length_mm`? Use flipper length to predict bill length, then predict bill length for flippers of 190, 200, and 210 mm
2.  **Part 3 steps:** Does `bill_depth_mm` differ across `species`? Check the equal-variance assumption, run the ANOVA, then Tukey's HSD

::: {.fragment style="font-size:90%"}
Check:

1.  $r$ = .65 (strong, positive); $b$ = 0.25 mm of bill per mm of flipper, $t$(331) = 15.69, $p$ \< .001; predicted bill lengths: 41.20, 43.75, 46.29 mm
2.  $F$(2, 330) = 344.8, $p$ \< .001; Gentoo bills are shallower than both Adelie and Chinstrap bills (both $p$ \< .001); Adelie vs. Chinstrap is not significant ($p$ = .897)
:::

## Must-Take-Home Message {style="font-size:90%"}

::: subpoint
○ **Correlation:** `cor(x, y)` → sign = direction, $|r|$ = strength; always check the scatterplot
:::

::: subpoint
○ **Regression:** `lm(y ~ x)` → slope = change in predicted *y* per 1-unit increase in *x*; `predict()` for new values
:::

::: subpoint
○ **Paired *t*:** one difference score per person, $df = n - 1$, $d = \bar{d} / s_d$
:::

::: subpoint
○ **ANOVA:** `aov(y ~ group)`, $MS = SS / df$, $F = MS_{between} / MS_{within}$, then `TukeyHSD()` to see which groups differ
:::

::: subpoint
○ Every test: hypotheses → decision → conclusion in words
:::
